title: JZ-motion: explainers, fast (about this app, with edit demo)

elements.text: an LLM-first studio for explainer videos

beats.title: Logo
beats.notes:
Hi, it's Jakub here
This is a showcase of application built by me in last couple of weeks. It is LLM first - explainer video creator.

beats.title: What it is
beats.notes: Everything you'll see here was drawn by it: a glowing marker board, animated text & graphics beat by beat, with an LLM doing most of the work.

elements.text:
what if the board
drew itself?

beats.title: Ideas, more than time
beats.notes: I have far more ideas than videos. I write notes, sometimes a full script…

beats.title: A video, planned
beats.notes: …then I'd plan a video to go with the script. Action, lights, the whole thing.

beats.title: No time
beats.notes: And then it stops. Recording, drawing, editing, publishing — I never have the time. Another month gone, and nothing shipped.

beats.title: What if the board drew itself?
beats.notes: So the question became: what if the board could draw itself, and a model could help me write it?

elements.text:
when you publish often,
keeping a consistent style matters

beats.title: Consistency matters
beats.notes: When you publish often, keeping a single style matters: viewers recognise it, you spend time on the idea, not the look.

beats.title: The reference
beats.notes: When I picked a style, I took inspiration from IBM Technology's lightboard explainers: one person, a glass board, neon diagrams.

beats.title: Clear, calm, fast to follow
beats.notes: Three qualities to copy: clear, calm, fast to follow.

beats.title: Home
beats.notes: It starts like a chat. One box in the middle of the screen.

beats.title: Just a sentence
beats.notes: I type what I want to explain, one sentence is enough, and a model drafts the whole presentation: scenes, drawings, beats and speaker notes.

beats.title: Three ways in
beats.notes: I can start from a topic, from a script I already wrote, or from a recording: then it transcribes me and cues every beat to the moment I say it.

beats.title: A model per job
beats.notes: And each way of starting can use a different model. More on why that matters in a minute.

beats.title: The editor
beats.notes: The draft opens in the editor. One window: the board in the middle, scenes and the library on the left, properties on the right.

beats.title: The board
beats.notes: The board itself is the drawing surface. Everything on it is written, drawn, or placed by me or by the AI.

beats.title: Beats under it
beats.notes: Under the board is the storyboard. Each card is a beat: one click while I present, with its actions laid out on a small timeline.

beats.title: Properties on the right
beats.notes: Everything has properties — positions and sizes like a drawing program, colours as marker tips, styles as little pictures.

beats.title: Scenes and library on the left
beats.notes: On the left: the list of scenes, and under it the library — icons, clipart, 3D models I can drop onto the board.

beats.title: A real editor
beats.notes: This is the editor you just saw, running on my laptop. Nothing drawn by hand here — it's a recording of a scratch board.

beats.title: Watch the headline
beats.notes: Watch the headline — I'll click on it and the properties panel on the right will pick up a marker.

beats.title: Click, pick a marker
beats.notes: A click selects it. Hover a colour in the marker tray and the text redraws itself in that ink.

beats.title: Then double-click to edit
beats.notes: The same element: a double-click opens it for editing, same handwriting, same position. Type what you want and press Enter.

beats.title: Hold the frame
beats.notes: Set play to off and the clip holds its last frame. That's how I keep talking without the UI moving behind me.

beats.title: A still frame to start
beats.notes: Any screen recorder gives you an APNG, GIF or animated WebP. On the board it sits like a screenshot: on its first frame, waiting.

beats.title: Watch the Script button
beats.notes: Watch the Script button — this clip starts in the editor and the first click lands there.

beats.title: Play on cue
beats.notes: A play action starts it from the beginning, in sync with my narration. Slow enough that the viewer actually sees each step.

beats.title: Pause to explain
beats.notes: Set on to false and the clip holds a frame, so you can talk over the result before moving on.

beats.title: This clip is jz-motion
beats.notes: In case it wasn't obvious: this is a recording of jz-motion itself, played back inside a jz-motion presentation. Both made from the same tools.

beats.title: LLM first
beats.notes: Under the hood, jz-motion is LLM first. A presentation is not pixels: it's one JSON document.

beats.title: Context
beats.notes: Every request sends the model the format reference, the drawing rules and the whole library: every icon, logo, clipart and 3D model it may use.

beats.title: Repair
beats.notes: …and if anything is wrong, the exact errors go back to the model to fix. That loop is why even small, cheap models produce something that loads.

beats.title: Board
beats.notes: Only valid JSON reaches the board, and from there it's all deterministic drawing.

beats.title: The JSON
beats.notes: And because it's plain JSON, I can read it, diff it, keep it in git, or edit it by hand.

elements.text: six marker colours · one stroke · drawn in order

beats.title: Same markers
beats.notes: The other promise is consistency. Whatever a model makes has to look like it came from the same set of markers.

beats.title: Everything
beats.notes: Icons, clipart, isometric 3D, charts, text: the same six colours, the same stroke, drawn in the order a person would draw them.

beats.title: Six marker colours
beats.notes: Green, pink, yellow, cyan, orange, white. Two to four per scene, each with a consistent meaning.

beats.title: Make your own
beats.notes: When the library doesn't have something, I describe it, and the model draws it under the same rules. The rules are shown, and every reply is checked.

beats.title: Versions
beats.notes: It's a conversation: every reply is a version. 'Make it pink', 'add a fan on top'… until I like one.

beats.title: Keep it
beats.notes: Then I save it, and from then on it's part of the library, for me and for every model that writes a presentation.

elements.text:
one source of truth —
so the house style stays the same

beats.title: One folder of skills
beats.notes: The skills folder is where I keep the rules: how to make a presentation, how to change one, how to draw a library item, how to demo an interface, how to turn it into a video.

beats.title: Both AIs follow them
beats.notes: The AI inside the app reads these files; Claude Code outside the app reads them too. So whichever one writes a scene, the style stays the same.

beats.title: One source of truth
beats.notes: Change the skill, change the output — on either side. That's how consistency survives.

scenes.title: A library that lowers the cost

beats.title: A shelf of pieces
beats.notes: The library is the shelf of pieces every explainer draws from: icons, logos, hand-drawn clipart, 3D models — every one checked against the house style.

beats.title: Each explainer adds one
beats.notes: When a presentation needs something new, I describe it, the model draws it under the same rules, and it joins the shelf.

beats.title: So each one costs less
beats.notes: Reusing is free; generating costs tokens. More in the library means fewer new items each time — and every explainer costs less than the one before.

beats.title: Overview
beats.notes: Here's how it fits together.

beats.title: In the browser
beats.notes: In the browser: a React editor, the board itself as SVG animated with GSAP, and the AI chat panels. Same code renders every export frame.

beats.title: A small local server
beats.notes: Next to it, a small local server with a few focused jobs: keep the files, proxy LLM calls, generate voice, transcribe recordings, export MP4s.

beats.title: Swappable models
beats.notes: The LLM is swappable: Claude, or anything OpenAI-compatible through OpenRouter, my own GPUs, or Ollama locally.

beats.title: Voice both ways
beats.notes: Voice goes both ways: an OpenAI TTS model generates narration from the script; an OpenAI transcription model turns a recorded script back into timed text.

scenes.title: The right model for each job

beats.title: Right job
beats.notes: Because every request is checked and repaired, I don't need the biggest model for everything.

beats.title: Story
beats.notes: A strong model writes the story: the structure, the scenes, the words.

beats.title: Small edits
beats.notes: Small edits, like changing a beat, work fine with a fast, cheap model like Haiku.

beats.title: Drawings
beats.notes: Icons, charts and 3D models are small, strict JSON. Haiku plus the rules is enough, and the library means most are never generated twice.

beats.title: Voice
beats.notes: A tiny OpenAI text-to-speech model generates narration from the script — fast, cheap, good enough to iterate on timing.

beats.title: Transcription
beats.notes: And when I record myself talking, Whisper transcribes it, so I can start a whole presentation from a recording — scenes cued to the moments I spoke.

elements.text:
I work on the words
independently from the board —
the board follows what I write.

beats.title: Script at the centre
beats.notes: The script is the centre of this app. Every scene, every beat, every spoken sentence lives in one place.

beats.title: Three ways to touch it
beats.notes: I can read and edit the whole thing in the Script view, or inline in the Timing prompter, or in the raw JSON tab if I want to see the shape.

beats.title: Same text, three lenses
beats.notes: It's one file; three views on the same text. I pick whichever one fits what I'm doing right now.

elements.text: each sentence on its own line, huge and readable
its target time, from the voice clip
timeline + playhead keep you honest as you read
no guessing the pace — I just read

beats.title: The prompter
beats.notes: This is the Timing window in prompter mode. The script lives here, blown up large, with every tool for keeping the pace right.

beats.title: Each sentence, its own line
beats.notes: Every sentence of the beat shows on its own line, big and readable from a distance. I don't lose my place when I look up at the camera.

beats.title: A target time per line
beats.notes: Next to each sentence, its target duration — pulled from a short voice clip the text-to-speech model generates. I know exactly how long each line should take.

beats.title: A clock that keeps me honest
beats.notes: At the bottom, a timeline shows where I am in the whole thing. The playhead moves as I read; a glance tells me if I'm fast, slow, or on it.

beats.title: Just read
beats.notes: Pull back and press record. No guessing the pace, no re-doing takes because I rushed one beat — I just read.

scene-ask bar: 'change THIS scene', keep the rest
AI tab: chat about the whole presentation

beats.title: AI, wherever I am
beats.notes: The AI isn't one feature — it's everywhere in the app. On the home screen to start, and inside the editor in two places.

beats.title: A sentence to a draft
beats.notes: From the home screen I pick a mode — topic, script, or recording — and a model, and go from one sentence to a whole first draft.

beats.title: Change THIS scene
beats.notes: Inside the editor, every scene has an ask bar above the storyboard. Describe one change — 'split this beat', 'add a database' — and only that scene changes.

beats.title: Chat about the whole thing
beats.notes: And on the AI tab in the right panel, a chat for bigger changes — picking models, running agent mode, watching every step land in the file.

beats.title: Same skills everywhere
beats.notes: All three read the same skills in dot-claude slash skills. Pick the place that fits the move — the house style follows.

elements.text: for a 10-minute video, start to finish

beats.title: The number
beats.notes: The whole point of this stack is: a ten-minute explainer under five dollars, start to finish.

beats.title: Why it works
beats.notes: Three reasons: a presentation is pure JSON, so the tokens are cheap; the library grows, so most drawings are reused; and the repair loop lets me use small, fast models.

beats.title: Record
beats.notes: And the last mile: I click Record and present, like I'm doing now. My voice, my camera and every click are saved as a take.

beats.title: Export
beats.notes: It exports straight to an MP4, with my camera in the corner or side by side with a friend. Or I record first, and it builds the presentation from the transcript.

beats.title: Thanks
beats.notes: That's jz-motion: explainers in minutes, in one consistent style, a little cheaper every time. Thanks for watching.
